title: Edom's Pride and the Day of the LORD
summary: Obadiah announces that God will bring down Edom, the nation descended from Esau, whose pride trusted in its mountain strongholds. Edom's crime was its conduct toward its brother Judah on the day Jerusalem fell: it stood aloof, gloated, looted, and handed over the refugees. The Day of the LORD is near for all nations, deliverance will come on Mount Zion, and the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
story: Obadiah comes, on the most common reading, from the dark years after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. The temple was burned, the king was captured, and many of the people were taken to Babylon. The story of Israel seemed to be over. Into that grief Obadiah speaks about one particular wound: the betrayal of Judah by Edom, its nearest kin. The feud reaches back to Genesis, where the twins Jacob and Esau struggle in the womb (Genesis 25:22-23) and Esau vows to kill his brother (Genesis 27:41). Obadiah moves that old story forward: the brother who should have helped chose to profit, and God has seen it. The chapter ends by lifting the reader's eyes past Edom to God's reign over all the nations.
historical:
Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea, in high, rocky country whose towns were hard to attack. Its people descended, according to Genesis 36, from Esau. David subdued Edom (2 Samuel 8:13-14), but it broke free of Judah in the ninth century (2 Kings 8:20-22), and the two peoples fought on and off for generations.

Most scholars date Obadiah shortly after 587 or 586 BC because verses 11 to 14 match what other texts say about Edom during the Babylonian conquest. Psalm 137:7 remembers the Edomites crying, as Jerusalem fell, to tear it down to its foundations; Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 25:12-14 and 35:1-15 condemn Edom for its part in Judah's ruin. A minority of scholars date the book to the reign of Jehoram of Judah (about 848 to 841 BC), when Edom revolted and Philistines and Arabs plundered Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 21:8-17). Verses 1 to 9 closely resemble Jeremiah 49:7-22, which suggests either that one prophet used the other or that both drew on a shared oracle. Edom's own decline followed within a century or two of the fall of Jerusalem; by the time of Malachi (Malachi 1:2-4) its land lay desolate, and Edomites had moved into southern Judah, later called Idumea.
cultural:
Edom's confidence came from geography. Its settlements perched on high plateaus and in rock-cut positions, so its people could believe, as verse 3 puts it, that no one could bring them down. The word for rock in verse 3 is sela, which was also the name of an Edomite stronghold (2 Kings 14:7); some have linked it with the later Nabatean city of Petra, though that identification is uncertain. Edom was also famous for wisdom. Teman, one of its districts, is praised for wisdom in Jeremiah 49:7, and Eliphaz, one of Job's counselors, was a Temanite (Job 2:11). Obadiah's promise to destroy "the wise men of Edom" (verse 8) strikes at the nation's pride in its sages.

In the ancient Near East, treaties between peoples were often described as brotherhood, and actual kinship carried obligations of protection. "Those who eat your bread" (verse 7) were allies bound by a shared meal, a sign of covenant loyalty. Casting lots for a captured city (verse 11) was the victors' way of dividing its spoils and its people. Standing at the crossroads to cut off fugitives (verse 14) means guarding the escape routes to catch refugees fleeing the burning city and handing them over to the conquerors.
literary: Obadiah is an oracle against a foreign nation, a common prophetic form. It moves in three stages. Verses 1 to 9 announce Edom's fall, using images of height brought low (the eagle's nest among the stars) and of total plunder (thieves leave something; grape pickers leave gleanings; Edom's conquerors will leave nothing). Verses 10 to 14 give the reason, in a series of eight prohibitions addressed to Edom as if the prophet were standing beside it on the day of Jerusalem's fall, each ending with a form of "in the day of their disaster". The word "day" occurs twelve times in the chapter. Verses 15 to 21 widen the scene to the Day of the LORD for all nations and end with Israel restored and God reigning. The whole book turns on reversal: "As you have done, it will be done to you" (verse 15).

outline.t: The nations summoned against Edom's proud heights
Edom stripped bare, betrayed by allies, its wise men destroyed
The charge: what Edom did on its brother's day of disaster
The Day of the LORD for all the nations
Deliverance on Mount Zion; the kingdom is the LORD's

doctrines.note: God judges nations for how they treat others, especially the vulnerable. The principle of verse 15, "As you have done, it will be done to you", shows judgment as fitting: Edom's deeds return upon its own head.

Edom's mountain security means nothing before God: "even from there I will bring you down" (verse 4). The nations rise and fall under his hand, and the book ends by declaring that the kingdom belongs to the LORD.
For a people who had lost city, temple, and king, Obadiah promises deliverance on Mount Zion and the return of the exiles. The hope does not rest on Judah's strength but on God's rule.

words.note: Zadon, arrogance or presumption. "The pride of your heart has deceived you" (verse 3). The word describes a pride that overreaches, and Proverbs 11:2 and 13:10 link it with disgrace and strife. For Obadiah, arrogance is self-deception: Edom believed its own boast about being unreachable.

Ach, brother. The word appears in verses 10 and 12 and carries the weight of the whole book. Edom and Israel were brother nations, descended from twins. Deuteronomy 23:7 told Israel not to despise an Edomite, "for he is your brother". Obadiah's charge is heavier because the betrayal was by kin.

Yom, day. Used twelve times in this short chapter. It names Judah's day of misfortune, destruction, and distress (verses 11 to 14), and then the Day of the LORD, which is near for all nations (verse 15). Edom's gloating on Judah's day will be answered on God's day.

Melukah, kingship or kingdom. The key word of the book's final line:"the kingdom will belong to the LORD" (verse 21). After Judah's king has been taken and Edom's pride destroyed, the true kingship is revealed as God's.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic. Obadiah's closing promise, that the kingdom will belong to the LORD, is the hope that Jesus announced had come near in his own ministry (Mark 1:15). The long quarrel between Jacob and Esau also reaches into the New Testament: Herod the Great, who tried to kill the infant Jesus, came from an Idumean (Edomite) family, and Paul uses Jacob and Esau to discuss God's purposes in Romans 9. But Obadiah's deepest connection to Christ may be moral. Edom stood aloof on its brother's day of disaster; Jesus came near to those in ruin, and in his parable it is the foreigner, the Samaritan, who stops at the roadside where others passed by (Luke 10:30-37). The gospel does not simply condemn the Edom in every human heart; it offers a brother who does not stand aside.

hard.q: Is Obadiah simply a nationalist cry for revenge against Israel's rival?
hard.a: Some readers find Obadiah uncomfortable because it rejoices in the downfall of another people. Several points help. First, the charge is specific and moral: violence against a brother, looting, gloating, and handing refugees over to their killers (verses 10 to 14). Second, the vengeance belongs to God, not to Judah's armies, and it follows the principle of just retribution that applies to Israel too; Amos, whose book precedes Obadiah, condemned Israel for the same kinds of sin. Third, the horizon is wider than Edom: the Day of the LORD is "near for all the nations" (verse 15), and the book ends with God's kingship, not Judah's. Some interpreters still note the tension between Obadiah's tone and Jesus' command to love enemies, and they read the book as the honest cry of victims placed in God's hands rather than as a model for personal revenge. Others see it as a necessary word that God does not ignore atrocities.

questions: Edom's guilt began with standing aloof. When have you stood by while someone else suffered, and what would it have meant to act?
Edom trusted its high places and its wise men. What do you trust to keep you out of reach of trouble?
How does the book's final line, that the kingdom will belong to the LORD, change the way you think about injustice you cannot fix?
